**Vignette: Marcus**

Marcus is nineteen years old and works the closing shift at a fast food restaurant on the outskirts of a mid-sized city in the American Midwest. He is quiet in the way that young men sometimes are when they have seen something they cannot unsee — not shy, exactly, but careful, as though he has learned that the world can shift without warning and he would rather not be caught off guard.

Fourteen months ago, a tornado tore through the town where Marcus grew up. He was seventeen at the time, living with his mother and younger sister in a single-story house on a flat stretch of residential street that offered nothing to slow the wind. The warning sirens came late. Marcus remembers grabbing his sister by the wrist and pulling her toward the bathroom, the only interior room without windows, and then the sound — a sound he still struggles to describe, settling on *everything at once* — and the sensation of the walls breathing inward before part of the roof lifted away. The three of them survived. The house did not. A neighbor two doors down did not either.

In the weeks that followed, Marcus and his family stayed with relatives in another part of the state. He finished his senior year at a new school, distracted and disconnected, and after graduation took the job at the restaurant because it was close to the apartment he now shares with a cousin. He tells himself he is doing fine. He tells himself this often enough that he almost believes it.

The trouble comes in layers. At work, the exhaust fan above the grill runs loud, and on certain nights — when it cycles up to a higher pitch — Marcus feels his chest tighten and his hands go cold. He keeps moving, bagging orders, wiping down the counter, because stopping feels more dangerous than the sensation itself. His coworkers think he is a hard worker. He is, in part, because standing still gives the feeling too much room.

Sleep is its own problem. He falls asleep without much difficulty but wakes in the early hours with his heart already running, the details of the dream dissolving before he can name them, leaving only the residue of dread. Some nights he gets up and sits by the window, watching the sky. He has downloaded three different weather apps on his phone. He checks them before bed, when he wakes, and during his breaks at work. When a storm system appears on the radar — even a routine one, even one that will bring nothing more than rain — he spends the day in a state of low-grade alertness that exhausts him by evening.

He has not been back to his hometown. His mother has asked him to come for holidays and he finds reasons not to. He does not explain this to her because he does not fully understand it himself, only that the thought of standing on that street produces something close to nausea. He has stopped watching certain movies — anything with wind, anything with destruction, anything that shows a sky turning green. He muted the word *tornado* on social media and then felt faintly embarrassed about it, as though he were being dramatic.

What Marcus finds hardest to articulate is the way the event has changed his relationship with ordinary things. A cloudy afternoon is no longer just a cloudy afternoon. A loud truck passing the restaurant window requires a moment of recalibration. He describes feeling, at times, like he is watching his own life from slightly outside of it, going through the motions of being nineteen — joking with coworkers, scrolling his phone, eating fast food on his break — while some other part of him remains crouched in a bathroom with his sister, waiting to find out what will be left.

He is not sure what he is waiting for now. He is not sure the waiting has stopped.
